exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 15–20, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer. Unless stated otherwise, $$B$$ is a basis for a vector space $$V$$ .

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$V$$ and if $$B$$ contains $$n$$ vectors, then the $$B \text{-coordinate}$$ vector of $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .
(T/F) If $$B$$ is the standard basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then the $$B \text{-coordinate}$$ vector of an $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is $$\mathbf{x}$$ itself.
(T/F) If $$P_{B}$$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix, then $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{\textbf{B}} = P_{\textbf{B}}\mathbf{x}$$ , for $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ .
(T/F) The correspondence $$\mathbf{\lbrack x\rbrack}_{B}\mapsto\mathbf{x}$$ is called the coordinate mapping.
(T/F) The vector spaces $${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$$ and $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ are isomorphic.
(T/F) In some cases, a plane in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ can be isomorphic to $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ .

The vectors $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 8} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{3} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ span $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ but do not form a basis. Find two different ways to express $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ as a linear combination of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ .

Let $$B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1} \text{,} \ldots\mathbf{b}_{n} \right\}$$ be a basis for a vector space $$V$$ . Explain why the $$B \text{-coordinate}$$ vectors of $$\mathbf{b}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{b}_{n}$$ are the columns $$\mathbf{e}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{n}}$$ of the $$n \times n$$ identity matrix.

Let $$S$$ be a finite set in a vector space $$V$$ with the property that every $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ has a unique representation as a linear combination of elements of $$S$$ . Show that $$S$$ is a basis of $$V$$ .

Suppose $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4} \right\}$$ is a linearly dependent spanning set for a vector space $$V$$ . Show that each $$\mathbf{w}$$ in $$V$$ can be expressed in more than one way as a linear combination of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4}$$ . [Hint: Let $$\mathbf{w} = k_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + k_{4}\mathbf{v}_{4}$$ be an arbitrary vector in $$V$$ . Use the linear dependence of $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4} \right\}$$ to produce another representation of $$\mathbf{w}$$ as a linear combination of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4}$$ .]

Let $$B = \left\{ {\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 4} \end{array} \right\rbrack \text{,} \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 9 \end{array} \right\rbrack} \right\}$$ . Since the coordinate mapping determined by $$B$$ is a linear transformation from $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ into $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ , this mapping must be implemented by some $$2 \times 2$$ matrix $$A$$ . Find it. [Hint: Multiplication by $$A$$ should transform a vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ into its coordinate vector $$\mathbf{\lbrack x\rbrack}_{B}$$ .]

Let $$B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1} \text{,} \ldots\mathbf{b}_{n} \right\}$$ be a basis for $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Produce a description of an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ that implements the coordinate mapping $$\left. \mathbf{x}\mapsto\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B} \right.$$ . (See Exercise 25.)

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 27–30 concern a vector space $$V$$ , a basis $$\textbf{B} =$$ $$\left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{b}_{n} \right\}$$ , and the coordinate mapping $$\left. \mathbf{x}\mapsto\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B} \right.$$ .

problem.paragraph: Show that the coordinate mapping is one-to-one. [Hint: Suppose $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{u} \right\rbrack_{B} = \left\lbrack \mathbf{w} \right\rbrack_{B}$$ for some $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{w}$$ in $$V$$ , and show that $$\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{w}$$ .]

Show that the coordinate mapping is onto $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . That is, given any $$\mathbf{y}$$ in $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , with entries $$y_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} y_{n}$$ , produce $$\mathbf{u}$$ in $$V$$ such that $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{u} \right\rbrack_{B} = \mathbf{y}$$ .

Show that a subset $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ in $$V$$ is linearly independent if and only if the set of coordinate vectors $$\left\{ \left\lbrack \mathbf{u}_{1} \right\rbrack_{B}, \text{…} \text{,} \left\lbrack \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\rbrack_{B} \right\}$$ is linearly independent in $$\mathbf{R}^{n}$$ . [Hint: Since the coordinate mapping is one-to-one, the following equations have the same solutions, $$c_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} c_{p}$$ .] $$c_{1} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{u}_{p} & = & 0 & \text{The} \text{zero} \text{vector} \text{in} V \left[c_{1} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{u}_{p}\right]_{B} & = & \left[0\right]_{B} & \text{The} \text{zero} \text{vector} \text{in} \mathbb{R}^{n}$$

Given vectors $$\mathbf{u}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p}$$ , and $$\mathbf{w}$$ in $$V$$ , show that $$\mathbf{w}$$ is a linear combination of $$\mathbf{u}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p}$$ if and only if $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{w} \right\rbrack_{B}$$ is a linear combination of the coordinate vectors $$\left(\left[\right. \mathbf{u}_{1} \left]\right.\right)_{B} , \ldots , \left( [ \mathbf{u}_{p} ]\right)_{B} .$$

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 41 and 42 concern the crystal lattice for titanium, which has the hexagonal structure shown on the left in the accompanying figure. The vectors $$\begin{bmatrix} 2.6 \\ - 1.5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 4.8 \end{bmatrix}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ form a basis for the unit cell shown on the right. The numbers here are $$Ångstrom$$ units $$\left( 1 \text{Å} \right. = 10^{- 8}$$ cm). In alloys of titanium, some additional atoms may be in the unit cell at the octahedral and tetrahedral sites (so named because of the geometric objects formed by atoms at these locations).

problem.paragraph: One of the octahedral sites is $$\begin{bmatrix} {1/2} \\ {1/4} \\ {1/6} \end{bmatrix},$$ relative to the lattice basis. Determine the coordinates of this site relative to the standard basis of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ .
One of the tetrahedral sites is $$\begin{bmatrix} {1/2} \\ {1/2} \\ {1/3} \end{bmatrix}.$$ Determine the coordinates of this site relative to the standard basis of $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ .

list.item: It is evident that the matrix $$P_{B} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{b}_{1} & \mathbf{b}_{2} & \mathbf{b}_{3} \end{bmatrix}$$ is row-equivalent to the identity matrix. By the Invertible Matrix Theorem, $$P_{B}$$ is invertible and its columns form a basis for $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ .
From part (a), the change-of-coordinates matrix is $$P_{B} = \left[\right. 1 & - 3 & 3 0 & 4 & - 6 0 & 0 & 3 \left]\right. .$$

To solve the equation in (c), it is probably easier to row reduce an augmented matrix than to compute $$P_{B}^{- 1}$$ : $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 & - 8 \\ 0 & 4 & - 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & - 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & P_{B} & & & x & & & & & I & & \left[x\right]_{B}$$ ﻿Hence $$\left(\left[\right. \mathbf{x} \left]\right.\right)_{B} = \left[\right. - 5 2 1 \left]\right.$$

problem.paragraph: The coordinates of $$\mathbf{p}(t) = 6 + 3t - t^{2}$$ with respect to $$B$$ satisfy $$c_{1} \left(1 + t\right) + c_{2} ( 1 + t^{2} ) + c_{3} ( 1 + t^{2} ) = 6 + 3 t - t^{2}$$
Equating coefficients of like powers of $$t$$ , we have $$c_{1} & + & c_{2} & & & = & 6 c_{1} & & & + & c_{3} & = & 3 & & c_{2} & + & c_{3} & = & - 1$$
Solving, we find that $$c_{1} = 5$$ , $$c_{2} = 1$$ , $$c_{3} = - 2$$ , and $$\left(\left[\right. \mathbf{p} \left]\right.\right)_{B} = \left[\right. 5 1 - 2 \left]\right. .$$
